title: Bell's Theorem and the 2022 Nobel Prize

cards.b: For 30 years after EPR, whether particles carry hidden "answers" from the start was thought to be a matter of philosophy. In 1964 John Bell, an Irish physicist at CERN, showed it can be tested. The tests say: no local hidden answers. The 2022 Nobel Prize in Physics honoured the experimenters who proved it.

A source sends one particle of an entangled pair to Alice and one to Bob. Each randomly picks one of two settings (angles) for their detector and records a result: +1 or -1. They then compare many rounds and compute a combined score.

The question: can any plan agreed in advance (like the gloves), with answers fixed at the source, beat a certain score?

Bell proved that if each particle carries pre-set answers and nothing travels between Alice and Bob (local realism), then correlations obey an inequality. The 1969 version by Clauser, Horne, Shimony and Holt (CHSH) is neat: the score S can be at most 2 for any local hidden plan.

Quantum theory predicts up to 2√2, about 2.83 (the Tsirelson bound), for entangled particles measured at well chosen angles.

Two students in separate rooms get different questions and must give answers that match in some cases and mismatch in others. If they agreed a strategy beforehand, they can win at most 75% of rounds. With entangled particles they can win about 85%. It is not that they communicate; they cannot. It is that no pre-agreed strategy reaches that score.

Where it breaks: students could cheat by signalling. In a real test, the choices are made too fast for any light-speed signal.

• Freedman and Clauser (1972): first test, violated the inequality.
  • Alain Aspect (1982): switched detector settings while photons were in flight.
  • Anton Zeilinger's group (Vienna): many refined tests, and entanglement over long distances.
  • 2015 loophole-free tests: Hensen et al. (Delft, electron spins 1.3 km apart), Giustina et al. (Vienna) and Shalm et al. (NIST).
  • 2018 Big Bell Test: about 100,000 volunteers around the world chose the settings.

The 2022 Nobel Prize in Physics went to Alain Aspect, John Clauser and Anton Zeilinger "for experiments with entangled photons, establishing the violation of Bell inequalities and pioneering quantum information science". John Bell died in 1990 and never received one.

Known

No theory in which particles have pre-set answers and nothing influences distant results can match the data. Quantum theory fits.

Interpretation

Give up locality (Bohm's pilot wave), give up that a single outcome occurs (many-worlds), or give up "free choice" (superdeterminism, a minority view). Each is a different story.

Nobody has to accept faster-than-light signals: Bell correlations carry no message.

• "Bell proved Einstein wrong about everything." Einstein was right that something must be added or given up. Bell showed which options remain.
  • "It proves faster-than-light influence." Only if you assume realism. Other options exist.
  • "The universe is not real." Only that local, pre-set values are ruled out.

Indian groups at ISI Kolkata, HRI Prayagraj, IMSc and RRI have worked on Bell inequalities and "device-independent" security, where certainty comes from a Bell violation alone. This underpins the quantum key distribution being developed under India's National Quantum Mission.

• Bell (1964), CHSH (1969): local hidden values give S ≤ 2; quantum gives up to 2.83.
  • Experiments (1972, 1982, 2015, 2018) violate the limit.
  • 2022 Nobel: Aspect, Clauser and Zeilinger.

Think about it

  1. Why did Aspect change the detector settings during flight?
  2. Why does a Bell violation not let us send messages faster than light?

o: Local hidden-variable theories make testable predictions
